finding: The new opening paragraph scores `blocking` 2 of 2 cycles in which it "would have shipped over an error row", then discharges that with "it is the reason the sink validation above is a precondition rather than a nicety". Sink validation cannot touch either miss. Both are rounds that would never have run: v0.35.0's error row is in audit-round-4.ndjson and `blocking` halts at round 3 (measured: error rows appear in that cycle only in rounds 1 and 4), and v0.36.0's is round 7's WriteSnapshotAtomic collision, four rounds past the same halt. Neither row's severity was wrong. Validating severity makes a label well-formed, never truthful, and cannot make an unrun round run. The release's strongest recorded argument against its own default is therefore answered by a mechanism orthogonal to it, in the sentence that lets the default stand. The paragraph also cites "the sink validation above"; that paragraph is thirty lines below it.
suggestion: Delete the discharge, or replace it with one that addresses the failure: what makes it safe to stop at round 3 when the two recorded misses were found at rounds 4 and 7. §2.0a names the only candidate on the table (ask the role whether it still holds its prior reasoning) and this release does not ship it, which is itself an argument for defaulting to `all`.

finding: The round-1 critical was only half repaired, and the surviving half is the sentence that justifies shipping. Commit c205812 rewrote one paragraph of §2 to say severity is NOT validated ('The field it reads exists and is NOT validated'; 'a self-declared judgement with nothing to check it against, which is scope's position, not role's'). Eight lines later the UNCHANGED paragraph 'This is not the deferred scope idea, and the distinction is the reason this ships' still reads: 'That objection does not touch severity -- it is an existing enum, VALIDATED AT THE SCHEMA, carried by every row already recorded.' That is the same false claim all four round-1 roles filed a critical on (architect prompt-text-read-as-validation, ax-economist unvalidated-agent-label-gates-release, implementer unvalidated-field-assumed-validated, tester unvalidated-enum-claim), restated verbatim in the one paragraph that carries the release's ship justification. It also contradicts the repaired paragraph directly: the repair says the scope objection DOES now touch severity, this paragraph says it does not. And 'carried by every row already recorded' is refuted by the repair's own evidence fifteen lines above -- 67 non-PASS rows carry out-of-enum severities (high 16, medium 15, low 36). A reader who stops at the bolded ship-justification paragraph gets exactly the falsified argument round 1 removed.
suggestion: Rewrite the 'This is not the deferred scope idea' paragraph on the repaired footing. The distinction that survives is not 'severity is validated and scope is not' -- it is that severity is an enum this release makes checkable at the sink whereas scope has no checkable referent at all. Delete 'validated at the schema' and 'carried by every row already recorded', and make the paragraph state that the sink validation earlier in §2 is what creates the asymmetry, not a pre-existing one.

finding: §2 never says whether audit_converge_on is evaluated LIVE against each recorded round's rows or only once, at record time, and the release's own claims split on the answer. Audit stores a boolean per round (audit_record.go:208) and engine.ConsecutiveClean (engine/reviewstate.go:429) walks stored flags; the review twin engine.ReviewConsecutiveClean (engine/reviewclean.go:115-128) reloads each round's rows through LoadRoundRows and recomputes, and its own doc comment closes with `audit sequences keep using ConsecutiveClean`. §7 test 4 replays NINE already-recorded v0.35.0 rounds whose stored Clean flags were computed under the any-non-PASS rule, and §2.1 claims `all` `reproduces the recorded history exactly` -- both statements are only meaningful under live recomputation. A record-time-only implementation passes tests 2 and 3 unchanged and fails 4, and switching the knob mid-cycle would silently do nothing to rounds already on disk (v0.31.0 test 4 pins the opposite for review). This is the release's central function and the implementer would have to pick it.
suggestion: State it the way v0.31.0 §3.4 states the review rule -- `recomputed live per round` -- and say which symbol the release adds or changes: a new engine.AuditConsecutiveClean/AuditRoundClean pair mirroring reviewclean.go, or a severity-aware ConsecutiveClean (see the Non-Goal 4 collision reported separately). Then say what the stored Clean flag means afterwards for audit, since nothing may read it.

finding: §2 states two mutually exclusive mechanisms for the same input, in adjacent sentences, and cites as precedent a section that does the opposite of what it proposes. Sentence one: a non-PASS row whose severity is missing or outside `error | warning | info` `is rejected by --record the way an unknown category is` -- i.e. countAuditFindings aborts the whole file and the round is never recorded (audit_record.go:62-70 exits ExitValidation on the parse/validation path; invalidCategoryRows.err() at :289 is that shape). Sentence two: `The conservative rule for an unrecognised value must be stated normatively and must fail closed -- v0.31.0 §4.1 states its review counterpart that way`. v0.31.0 §4.1 does not reject anything: it reads `A surviving finding whose severity is missing or, after normalization, outside critical|high|medium|low is treated conservatively as blocking`. Rejection and treat-as-blocking are different mechanisms with different exit codes, different failure modes under TP_UNATTENDED, and different consequences for the corpus. Worse, under rejection there is by construction no unrecognised value left for a fail-closed rule to govern on any newly recorded round -- the only rows the rule could ever apply to are ones already on disk, which is precisely the migration §2 defers.
suggestion: The release needs both and should say so as two tasks: (1) sink rejection at --record for newly submitted non-PASS rows, with its exit code and hint; (2) v0.31.0 §4.1's treat-as-blocking rule for the streak walk, which is what governs already-recorded rounds and rows a rejection can no longer reach. Stop citing §4.1 as precedent for (1); it is precedent for (2).

finding: The repair to §2.1's v0.36.0 row corrected a stale round count and, in the same edit, replaced a CORRECT cell with a false one. Round 1 said the row was stale ('7 and open'); the repair wrote '13, converged | round 3 | round 13'. Measured from spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/state.json and audit-round-1..13.ndjson: every one of the thirteen recorded rounds has clean=false and a non-zero non-PASS count (22,8,11,10,9,6,10,3,4,2,1,2,3). Round 13 carries 3 non-PASS rows, two of them severity error. So under `all` with audit_clean_rounds:2 the v0.36.0 cycle NEVER converges across its recorded rounds -- the old cell's 'not yet' was right and 'round 13' is wrong. 'converged' in the rounds-recorded column is unsupported the same way: no recorded round is clean, so consecutive_clean is 0 at round 13, which is exactly what §2.0a still says two paragraphs earlier ('consecutive_clean never left zero') and what the just-deleted §5 tabulated (rounds 10-13: consecutive_clean 0,0,0,0). The repair is self-refuting on the same page: §2's new lead paragraph states that v0.36.0's rounds 12 and 13 each carry error rows, which is incompatible with `all` converging at round 13. The evidence that would have caught this -- §5's round 10-13 table -- was deleted by commit 9864b00 in the same batch.
suggestion: Restore the truthful cell: v0.36.0 rounds recorded '13, not converged'; converges under `all` 'not reached in 13 rounds'. Verify the blocking cells too (both check out: v0.35.0 r2/r3 and v0.36.0 r2/r3 each carry zero error rows). Then reconcile the surrounding prose, which currently reads v0.36.0 as a cycle that finished.

finding: The repaired v0.36.0 row is false on both of its numbers and contradicts two other sections of the same spec. The cell reads '13, converged' and 'converges under all | round 13'. Measured from spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/state.json, all 13 recorded audit rounds carry clean:false -- that cycle has never converged under the rule tp ships today, which is exactly the `all` predicate. Per-round surviving non-PASS rows (no audit row anywhere in the corpus carries a `resolved` key, so surviving == non-PASS): r8 3, r9 4, r10 2, r11 1, r12 2 (both error), r13 3 (2 error, 1 warning). With audit_clean_rounds: 2, `all` needs two consecutive zero-surviving rounds and v0.36.0 never reaches even one, so 'round 13' is unreachable rather than merely optimistic. §2.0a says the opposite of the cell in plain words -- 'consecutive_clean never left zero' -- and §2's own opening says rounds 7, 12 and 13 carry error rows, which cannot coexist with round 13 being an `all`-convergence. The row is load-bearing twice: it is half of 'the two cycles disagree', and it is the evidence for '`all` reproduces the recorded history exactly', which holds only for v0.35.0 (r8 and r9 are the only zero-surviving audit rounds in either cycle).
suggestion: Replace the cell with the measured outcome -- 'never converges under `all`; 13 rounds recorded, none clean' -- and scope the 'reproduces the recorded history exactly' claim to v0.35.0. If the column actually means 'the round the phase stopped at', rename it, because v0.36.0's stop was an operator decision rather than a predicate firing; and add the v0.36.0 replay to §7 test 4 so the cell is pinned by an assertion rather than by prose.

finding: The v0.36.0 row added this round is falsified by the data it claims to replay, on two of its three cells. Measured from spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/state.json: all 13 recorded audit rounds carry clean:false, so (a) the rounds-recorded cell '13, converged' is false -- that cycle has zero clean rounds and CLAUDE.md itself lists v0.36.0 as 'In flight'; and (b) under `all` (clean = no non-PASS row survives) NO round of the 13 qualifies -- audit-round-13.ndjson holds 84 rows of which 3 are non-PASS (2 error, 1 warning) -- so `all` never converges and the cell 'round 13' names a round that cannot be the answer. The paragraph directly under the table is what refutes it: if '`all` reproduces the recorded history exactly', and the recorded history is 'never converged', then the `all` cell must read 'never'. Only the blocking cell survives measurement: rounds 2 and 3 carry zero error rows, so blocking converges at round 3 with audit_clean_rounds:2 (clean-under-blocking rounds are 2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,11; 1, 7, 12 and 13 carry error). This is the table the release's single contested decision rests on, and a decomposer extending test 4's replay to the second row writes an assertion the corpus refutes.
suggestion: Write the row as '13, not converged | round 3 (r2, r3 carry zero error) | never (0 of 13 rounds are fully PASS; round 13 itself carries 2 error + 1 warning)'. Then extend test 4 to replay BOTH rows from the recorded rows, so the table is guarded by an executable assertion rather than restated prose -- the v0.36.0 row is the one the argument leans on and it is currently the untested half of the table.

finding: The v0.36.0 row is false in both load-bearing cells, and the round-1 repair is what introduced it: the cell read "7 and open" and now reads "13, converged | blocking round 3 | all round 13". Measured from spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/state.json, the cycle has thirteen recorded audit rounds and EVERY one carries clean: false, round 13 included (findings: 3). audit-round-13.ndjson holds three non-PASS rows, two of them severity error, and no row in that file carries a resolved key. So with audit_clean_rounds: 2 the trailing clean run is zero for the whole cycle: `all` has no convergence point there at all, and the cycle has converged in neither phase (review rounds 1-15 are also clean: false). This is the table carrying the one decision §2.1 itself calls contested, and the word "converged" reads as that case being closed.
suggestion: Re-derive the row from state.json's clean flags rather than from prose: 13 rounds recorded, zero clean, `all` never converges, `blocking` would converge at round 3. Saying that plainly strengthens §2.1's own conclusion that one sample each way is not a policy, instead of resting it on a cell that does not survive its own state file.

finding: §3's mechanism cannot reach the case §3 exists to fix, because an audit round's cleanliness is frozen at record time and a disposition is written after that. internal/cli/audit_record.go:71 computes `clean := findings == 0` and recordAuditRoundEntry (audit_record.go:205-215) STORES both `Findings` and `Clean` on the round entry; runAuditStatus (audit_record.go:329-344) and engine.ConsecutiveClean (engine/reviewstate.go:429-438) read that stored flag and never recompute it -- the contrast is explicit on the review side, where review_status.go:135 comments that `rounds[i].Clean above is the live severity-aware value`. tp audit --resolve writes `row["resolved"]` into the ALREADY-RECORDED round file (audit_resolve.go:78, :137), and the next round's merged file is built fresh from role files by loadAuditMergeRows/dedupAuditRows, so the same item re-reported in round N+1 carries no `resolved` key at all. Excluding wontfix/duplicate rows `from the round's finding count` at the record path therefore excludes nothing in the flow §3 describes: the disposition never exists when the count is taken, and never survives into the next round's file. The field cycle §3 cites -- accepted backlog items `correctly re-reported, round after round` -- is exactly this flow.
suggestion: Name which of the two mechanisms this release ships, because they are different tasks with different blast radii: (a) live recomputation of a recorded audit round's cleanliness from its own rows, the way engine.ReviewConsecutiveClean/ReviewRoundClean already do for review (this also makes the stored Clean flag advisory for audit and must say so); or (b) carry-forward of dispositions by (role,item_id) from the previous recorded round into the round being recorded, which needs a stated match rule and a stated behaviour when the item text changed. Neither is derivable from the current text.

finding: "a non-PASS row whose severity is missing or outside error | warning | info is rejected by --record the way an unknown category is" cites a sink that deliberately does the opposite on the missing case. internal/cli/audit_record.go:282 returns early when category == "", and internal/cli/audit_category_sink_test.go pins that behaviour in TestCountAuditFindings_AcceptsTheEnumAndAbsentCategory with its reason in the comment: PASS rows carry an explicit null, and "treating that as invalid would reject every clean round." Rejecting on absence is a strictly larger rule than the precedent named for it, so the spec inherits its shape from a citation that contradicts it.
suggestion: State the rule normatively instead of by analogy: which of absent, null and out-of-enum is refused, on which statuses, and note that this deviates from the category sink and why. If absence is to be refused, say so knowing the analogy's own guard test exists because the identical rule broke clean rounds on the sibling field.

finding: The new opening paragraph reports a score ('2 of 2 cycles in which blocking would have shipped over an error row, not 1 of 2') that §2.1 computes by a different rule three paragraphs later, so the number cannot be re-derived and two engineers score the same corpus differently. §2 counts every post-stop round carrying an error row: v0.35.0 round 4 (measured {error 1, warning 2, info 1} -- exact) and v0.36.0 rounds 7, 12, 13 (measured 3, 2, 2 error rows). §2.1 then discounts exactly that kind of row: 'Two are repair artifacts of round 6 and would not exist in a cycle that had stopped at round 3.' Apply §2.1's rule to §2's inputs and the score moves: v0.35.0's round-4 error row follows round 3's repairs and is a candidate artifact by the same test, and §2.0a says v0.36.0's rounds 12-13 rows were found 'only because those rounds were asked to build a new instrument rather than to re-read' -- a method change a cycle stopped at round 3 would never have made. Depending on which of the release's own rules a reader applies, the instrument reads 2 of 2, 1 of 2 or 0 of 2, and this is the number carrying the case against the release's single contested decision.
suggestion: State the counting rule once, before either paragraph uses it -- e.g. 'a post-stop error row counts against the default unless it is an artifact of a repair that a stopped cycle would not have made; rows produced by a change of method are counted' -- and then apply it to all four rounds explicitly (0.35.0 r4; 0.36.0 r7, r12, r13), showing the arithmetic. A score with no stated rule is not a measurement, and this one is the release's own evidence against its default.

finding: The new sink-validation sentence requires two opposite behaviours for the same case, so two engineers write contradictory tests and both can cite it. It reads: 'a non-PASS row whose severity is missing or outside error | warning | info is rejected by --record the way an unknown category is'. The shipped analogue does NOT reject a missing value: invalidCategoryRows.observe (internal/cli/audit_record.go:280-286) does `category, _ := row["category"].(string); if category == "" || engine.IsValidCategory(category) { return }`, so an absent key, a JSON null and a non-string value all take the early return and record cleanly; only a non-empty out-of-enum string is collected and aborts via ic.err() (:252-254, 289-295). An engineer implementing 'the way an unknown category is' therefore ships a validator that accepts exactly the missing severity the same sentence says must be rejected. The sentence also never separates 'missing' (key absent) from `severity: null`, which is a third case the schema line at audit_schema.go:24 explicitly legislates for PASS rows and which every recorded PASS row uses (measured: 0 PASS rows in the whole 10,435-row corpus carry a non-null severity).
suggestion: Drop the analogy as the normative carrier and enumerate the cases with a verdict each: key absent -> rejected; null on a non-PASS row -> rejected; non-string -> rejected; out-of-enum string -> rejected; null on a PASS row -> accepted. If the intent is deliberately stricter than the category sink, say so in the same sentence ('stricter than the category check, which exempts an absent value'), because as written the analogy asserts the opposite of the rule it is attached to.

finding: The rejection's price is a whole round each time, and it is measurable on this repository. countAuditFindings aborts the entire file at ExitValidation on the invalid-row tally (internal/cli/audit_record.go:62-68), and engine.IsValidCategory has exactly one caller, so --merge does not check: the refusal lands at the LAST sink, after every role has run and after merge. The 67 out-of-enum severity rows §2 counts are spread over fifteen recorded round files (0.29.0 r1-2, 0.30.0 r1, 0.31.0 r1, 0.31.2 r1-5, 0.32.0 r1-6). Under the proposed rule, fifteen of this repository's own audit rounds would have been refused outright, each discarding four roles' work over a label. Under `tp run` the authoring subagents have already exited when --record runs, so the recovery is a re-run of the round: the most expensive round-trip tp has, spent to punish the cheapest artifact in the row.
suggestion: Put the check where it is cheap and keep the expensive artifact. Validate in --merge as well, so one role's bad row is caught before the other three are spent; and make the sink coerce rather than refuse -- record the row, rank an unrecognised severity as blocking, emit a notice. That yields the fail-closed property §2 wants without ever discarding agent-authored finding text.

finding: The round-1 repair landed in §2 and was not propagated to §2.1, so the two adjacent sections now hand the decision-maker opposite tallies of the same evidence. §2 concludes 'the instrument scores 2 of 2 cycles in which `blocking` would have shipped over an `error` row, not 1 of 2'. §2.1's summary is unchanged and still reads 'v0.35.0 is the case for the release', 'v0.36.0 is the case against the default', and 'the two cycles disagree, and one sample each way is not a policy'. Under §2's own corrected count the cycles do not disagree and there is no sample in favour, so §2.1's closing instruction to decomposition -- 'treat the default as the one decision in this release with a recorded argument against it' -- rests on a tally the same release withdrew two paragraphs earlier. This is not a wording clash: the surviving argument for shipping `blocking` as the default was the 1-1 split, and that split no longer exists in the spec.
suggestion: Rewrite §2.1's three summary paragraphs to the 2-of-2 reading, or delete them and let §2's paragraph carry the conclusion alone. Then re-argue §2's 'Default. blocking' against the corrected tally, or change the default, so the release does not ship a default whose only stated support has been retracted.

finding: audit_converge_on makes "was this round clean" a function of a knob, while every recorded round already carries a clean bool stamped under whatever policy was active when it was recorded, and --status emits those rounds verbatim (internal/cli/audit_record.go:337-344 returns audit_rounds beside consecutive_clean). The review twin the section invokes already solved this and the spec never says so: engine.ReviewConsecutiveClean recomputes each round's cleanliness live from its rows under the current review_converge_on and ignores the stored bool, while audit's ConsecutiveClean reads it. §2 does not say which audit adopts, so an agent parsing --status can be handed audit_rounds[].clean: false on every round beside consecutive_clean: 2, with no rule for reconciling two answers to one question.
suggestion: Say audit follows the twin exactly -- cleanliness recomputed live per round from the recorded rows under the resolved audit_converge_on -- and say what the stored clean field becomes (retired, or documented as a record-time verdict no consumer reads). Put the disagreement case in §7.

finding: §2 makes sink validation a normative deliverable -- 'This release therefore ships validation at the sink before the gate reads the field: a non-PASS row whose severity is missing or outside error | warning | info is rejected by --record the way an unknown category is' -- and calls it 'this release's first job'. §6 Non-Goal 3 states the opposite: 'Changing severity's meaning or vocabulary. error | warning | info is unchanged; this release only reads it.' Rejecting input at `tp audit --record` is not reading it; it changes what the command accepts and can refuse a round file that records cleanly today. No other section acknowledges the deliverable: §1 names two things the release gives audit, §5 closes 'This release is §2, §3 and §4', and §7's eight tests cover convergence, disposition and the streak reset only. The release's most safety-critical clause is thus the one its overview, its non-goals and its test list all contradict or omit.
suggestion: Give the validation its own numbered section carrying the mechanism, the exit code and the hint; add a §7 test for a rejected row and for an accepted one; and narrow Non-Goal 3 to 'the vocabulary is unchanged -- what changes is that it is now enforced at the sink'. Update §1 and §5's closing sentence to the same count.

finding: §2 mandates both a sink that refuses any non-PASS row outside the enum AND a normative fail-closed rule for "an unrecognised value". If the first holds, the second is unreachable for every round recorded after this release: no unrecognised severity can reach the predicate, because --record refused the file carrying it. Its only live population is rows recorded before the release, or files that never passed the sink. The spec states both as requirements and scopes neither, so decomposition builds two mechanisms for one hazard and writes the second's test against a case the first makes impossible.
suggestion: Choose one. Either the sink refuses, and the fail-closed rule is stated as governing pre-existing rounds only (and §2 then owes what the gate does with the 67); or the predicate fails closed, and no refusal is needed -- one mechanism, no round-trips, the row survives with its finding text intact.

finding: §2 names the migration for the 67 out-of-enum rows as an obligation and never discharges it: `the 67 historical rows are what the migration path has to answer for`. That is not a deferral to another release -- it is this release's own blocker, because the moment `blocking` ships, the streak walk reads `severity` off rounds that already contain `high` 16, `medium` 15, `low` 36. Sink validation at --record is inert for every one of them: they are already recorded. Four incompatible answers are available and the spec picks none: (a) reject at read, which makes tp unable to report --status on its own v0.29.0-v0.32.0 history; (b) v0.31.0 §4.1's treat-as-blocking, which permanently marks those rounds dirty (harmless for closed cycles, decisive for any live cycle mid-upgrade); (c) normalise high/medium/low onto error/warning/info, a rewrite of recorded rows that §7 test 7's own principle (`does not delete or rewrite any recorded round`) argues against; (d) scope the predicate to rounds recorded at or after this release, which needs a marker on the round that does not exist (engine.ReviewRound carries IDScheme for exactly this kind of epoch question, engine/reviewstate.go:503). No task acceptance can be written until one is chosen.
suggestion: Pick one and state it normatively in §2, with a test in §7. If (d), name the stored marker and say what an unmarked pre-release round means; IsLegacyRound/IDScheme is the shipped precedent for an epoch flag on ReviewRound.

finding: §2 prescribes two mutually exclusive dispositions for the same input and then admits the rule is unstated. One sentence rejects the row at `--record`; the next says 'The conservative rule for an unrecognised value must be stated normatively and must fail closed -- v0.31.0 §4.1 states its review counterpart that way and this section did not.' Rejection and fail-closed treatment are different behaviours with different blast radii: rejection refuses the round file so the row never enters the corpus, while fail-closed accepts the row and counts it as blocking. They also give opposite answers about the 67 historical rows §2 cites in the next paragraph -- unrecordable under rejection, uniformly blocking under fail-closed. §2 assigns those rows to a 'migration path' that no section of this release defines and §6 does not defer.
suggestion: Choose one rule and state it normatively in §2: either (a) `--record` rejects the row, with the exit code and hint named and an explicit statement that already-recorded rounds are untouched, or (b) the row is accepted and an unrecognised severity counts as blocking. Add the matching §7 test, and either specify the migration path for the 67 rows or list it as a Non-Goal with its reason.

finding: §2.0a assumes an audit-side `nonblocking_open`: 'audit_converge_on=blocking would have converged that run at round 3-4 with the remaining rows surfaced as nonblocking_open -- nothing hidden'. That field is documented as review-only and explicitly never an audit field. spec/0.31.0.md §8.4: 'nonblocking_open is review-only (audit convergence has no non-blocking notion, §4.4) and is never an audit field'; skills/tp/REFERENCE.md line 634 repeats it in the --compact disposition list; internal/cli/harness_note_test.go:263 records it in the audit --compact test's comment. This release is precisely what creates a non-blocking notion for audit, so emitting the field may be the right outcome -- but §2.0a treats it as an existing surface instead of specifying it. No section says when audit emits it or what it counts, §6 does not record the reversal of 0.31.0 §8.4, §7 has no test, and REFERENCE.md's --compact list would have to change. As written, the sentence that carries 'nothing hidden' -- the reassurance that makes stopping early acceptable -- depends on a surface the release does not ship.
suggestion: Either add a numbered clause specifying the audit-side emission on the same condition as review (a clean round with surviving non-blocking rows), a §7 test, and an explicit note that it supersedes spec/0.31.0.md §8.4's 'never an audit field'; or remove the field name from §2.0a and describe the outcome without naming a surface this release does not create.

finding: §2.0a closes 'nothing hidden, and the gate answering the question the operator was actually asking. §5 records the same gap from the --check side.' Commit 9864b00 removed the §5 that recorded that gap. The bare '§5' now resolves, within this document, to 'What is deliberately not in this release, and why it was here three hours ago' -- a removal notice, not a record of the --check gap. The gap now lives at spec/0.46.0.md §8 (verified present). §2.0a is an unchanged section left pointing at a heading whose subject moved out from under it; a reader following the reference lands on the reason it was removed and concludes the gap is out of scope, which is the opposite of what the sentence asserts.
suggestion: Repoint to `spec/0.46.0.md` §8. Run the same sweep over the rest of the file: after a same-file section is deleted, every bare §n reference is suspect, because a bare §n always resolves to something.

finding: §2.0a states the release's payoff in terms of an output field that a shipped contract says can never be an audit field: `audit_converge_on=blocking would have converged that run at round 3-4 with the remaining rows surfaced as nonblocking_open`. spec/0.31.0.md §8.4 reads `nonblocking_open is review-only (audit convergence has no non-blocking notion, §4.4) and is never an audit field`, its test 18 pins it (`tp audit --status --compact ... nonblocking_open is never an audit field`), skills/tp/REFERENCE.md's --compact disposition line repeats it as `(review-only, emitted only on an accepted-open clean round)`, and internal/cli/harness_note_test.go:263 records the same rule in the audit compact test. In code the emitter exists only on the review paths (review_record.go:229-233, review_status.go:135-139) and is fed by engine.ReviewRoundNonBlockingOpen. So §2.0a's stated outcome requires a new audit field that §2's mechanism does not specify, §7 does not test, and §6 does not record as a reversal. This is the same shape as the §5b the release just removed for `reverses a contract ... without recording the reversal`.
suggestion: Either add the audit nonblocking_open as an explicit §2 mechanism with its own test and a recorded reversal of v0.31.0 §8.4/§4.4 (including the --compact disposition), or rewrite §2.0a to describe the outcome in terms this release actually produces -- the rows stay recorded and visible in the round file and in overlap_report, and the gate opens.

finding: The one error row §2.1 offers as NOT a repair artifact -- the single piece of evidence carrying the case against the default -- is described in the present tense as a live defect in shipped code, and it is already fixed in this tree. §2.1 says 'engine.WriteSnapshotAtomic builds its temporary file from a fixed final + ".tmp", so role units that REFERENCE.md runs parallel with their siblings collide and the loser's rename fails with ENOENT ... It is a defect in shipped code'. Measured: engine/reviewstate.go:378-391 delegates to writeFileAtomic, and writeFileAtomic (engine/runstate.go:255-271) calls os.CreateTemp(filepath.Dir(path), filepath.Base(path)+".*.tmp") -- a unique name per call -- then renames. The repair's own comment records the same round 7 and cites different figures from the spec's: 'six of eight siblings failing with ENOENT after the winner moved it away, and 24 of 80 through the real brief_command strings at eight-way concurrency', against the spec's '0/20 sequential and 5/40 parallel'. So a reader has one defect, two incompatible measured rates (24/80 vs 5/40), and a present-tense claim the file refutes. The historical argument survives -- the defect existed when round 7 ran, and blocking would have stopped at round 3 -- but only the historical form is true.
suggestion: Put the sentence in the past tense and name where it was fixed ('engine.WriteSnapshotAtomic built its temporary file from a fixed final + ".tmp" until it was moved onto writeFileAtomic; the collision is what round 7 caught'). Then reconcile the two rates or cite only the one the code comment pins, since a claim of the form 'measured at 5/40' that disagrees with the repair's own recorded 24/80 gives a later reader no way to tell which run either number came from.

finding: §2's new lead paragraph concludes 'the instrument scores 2 of 2 cycles in which blocking would have shipped over an error row, not 1 of 2' -- and §2.1's conclusion, which the repair did not touch, still says the opposite twice. Line 128: 'v0.35.0 is the case FOR the release'. Line 141: 'the two cycles disagree, and one sample each way is not a policy.' Under the repaired §2 the cycles do not disagree; both are cases against, and there is no sample the other way. §2.1's heading likewise still promises the measurement is 'in both directions' while §2 now says the table measures only one direction and supplies the other in prose. Decomposition is told in the same section both that the default has one recorded argument against it and that the evidence is 2-0 against it; those imply different defaults.
suggestion: Rewrite §2.1's closing two paragraphs to the 2-of-2 reading, or state plainly why 'blocking would have shipped over an error row' is not the same as 'the cycle argues against blocking' (e.g. because the r4 error row would have been caught by the next cycle). Either way one sentence has to go: 'the two cycles disagree' and '2 of 2' cannot both stand.

finding: "resets consecutive_clean to zero" describes mutating state that does not exist. consecutive_clean is derived: engine.ConsecutiveClean walks AuditRounds backwards over each round's stored Clean bool and is called at output time (internal/cli/audit_record.go:101 and :339); nothing persists it. The equivalent with zero new stored bytes and no write is to stop that walk at the first round whose spec_hash differs from its successor's -- ReviewRound already stores spec_hash per round. The derived form is idempotent under RecordRound's rewrite path, needs no payload mutation at --record, applies retroactively to cycles already recorded, self-corrects if the spec is reverted, and makes §7 test 7 ("does not delete or rewrite any recorded round") true by construction rather than by assertion.
suggestion: Restate §4's mechanism as a read-time rule on the streak walk -- the trailing clean run ends at a spec_hash boundary -- and let the payload field report that derivation rather than evidence a write.

finding: §4 adds a second staleness rule beside a shipped one and never says how they compose. tp already refuses to converge an audit sequence over a moved spec: engine.Converged (engine/reviewstate.go:509-511) is `ConsecutiveClean(rounds) >= required && !StateStale(rounds, currentHash)`, and StateStale (:443-448) compares the CURRENT spec hash against the LAST recorded round's. §4's rule is a different comparison -- pairwise, between consecutive recorded rounds -- and §4 states no effect on `stale`, on `converged`, or on the divergence signal. That last one is not hypothetical: engine/divergence.go:68-71 documents DivergenceInputs.Stale as condition 3 and says it `is false by construction on --record`, which is true only because staleness today is measured against the round just stored. A pairwise reset makes a spec movement observable at record time for the first time, so condition 3's by-construction reasoning no longer holds and ComputeAuditDivergence's five-condition contract has to be re-derived. §1's own field report (`--status reported the round as non-stale while the spec hash changed twice mid-audit`) is a description of StateStale's last-round-only comparison, so the two rules are answering the same question with different windows.
suggestion: State whether the pairwise reset feeds `stale`, whether `converged` gains a third term or is unchanged because the streak already went to zero, and whether divergence condition 3 keeps its `false by construction on --record` property. If it does not, say what replaces it.

finding: §4's mechanism has no target to mutate. `consecutive_clean` is not stored anywhere: it is derived on every read by engine.ConsecutiveClean(rounds) -- audit_record.go:101 on --record, audit_record.go:339 on --status, audit.go:352 for prompt generation, and engine/resume.go:87 through engine.Converged. `When tp audit --record sees a spec_hash different from the previous round's, it resets consecutive_clean to zero` therefore describes a write to a value that exists only as a fold over stored Clean flags. The two implementable readings differ observably and §7 cannot tell them apart: (i) make the trailing walk hash-aware so it stops at a round whose spec_hash differs from its predecessor -- the reset is then permanent and shows up identically on --record, --status, tp resume and divergence; (ii) stamp something on the recorded round at --record time -- which needs a new field on engine.ReviewRound that §4 never names, and has to be reconciled with test 7's `does not delete or rewrite any recorded round`. Test 6 asserts only the --record payload, so an implementation that zeroes the number in that one response while --status recomputes a non-zero streak one command later passes it.
suggestion: Say which. If (i), say so and note that ConsecutiveClean is the function being changed (see the Non-Goal 4 collision). If (ii), name the stored field and add a test asserting --status reports the same reset --record reported.

finding: Round 1's §5 findings were answered by deletion, and the deletion took a requirement with it that the rest of the release still depends on. The removed §5 carried the only clause requiring the severity distinction to reach the gate: 'audit_converge_on already separates which rows block; the same distinction has to reach --check, or --check stays an instrument nobody can ship on.' That clause is now in no release. Meanwhile §2.0a, unchanged, still sells the whole release on that outcome -- 'audit_converge_on=blocking would have converged that run at round 3-4 with the remaining rows surfaced as nonblocking_open ... the gate answering the question the operator was actually asking.' Measured: `nonblocking_open` exists only on the review side (internal/cli/review_status.go:137, internal/cli/review_record.go:231); there is no audit equivalent. And §7's eight tests are all phrased on the round finding count and --record -- none mentions --status --check. So as it now stands the release can ship a field that changes what --record counts while --status --check behaves exactly as it does today, and every test would pass. Deferring the two candidate shapes to 0.46.0 §8 was right; deferring the requirement that the field reach the gate was not.
suggestion: Add a clause to §2 stating that audit_converge_on governs every consumer of audit convergence -- --record, --status, --status --check and the resume/run oracle -- and name the audit-side surfacing key for the non-blocking survivors. Add a §7 test asserting a round whose only non-PASS rows are warning/info reaches --status --check exit 0 under blocking and exit 1 under all. What stays deferred to 0.46.0 §8 is WHICH ROLES the gate reads, not whether the severity policy reaches it.

finding: Non-Goal 3 and §2 now describe different releases, and a decomposer reading one would not write the task the other requires. Non-Goal 3: `Changing severity's meaning or vocabulary. error | warning | info is unchanged; this release only reads it.` §2, after the round-1 repair: `this release's first job` is validation at the sink, `a non-PASS row whose severity is missing or outside error | warning | info is rejected by --record`. First-time enforcement of an enum that has never been enforced is not `only reading it` -- it is a behaviour change to tp audit --record for every existing user, on a corpus that violates the enum 67 times by §2's own count, and it is the precondition §2 says makes the default safe. Under Non-Goal 3 the validation task does not exist; under §2 it is the first task in the release.
suggestion: Rewrite Non-Goal 3 to say what is actually out of scope -- the vocabulary and the meanings of the three values are unchanged -- and state in the same breath that enforcement of that vocabulary at the record sink is IN scope and is new behaviour. Add the enforcement to §1's summary of what the release ships, which currently promises only `a severity-aware convergence policy, and a reason to distrust a streak that spans a changed spec`.

finding: Non-Goal 3 was not updated when §2 was rewritten, and it now contradicts the release's own first job. It reads 'Changing severity's meaning or vocabulary. error | warning | info is unchanged; this release only reads it.' §2 now has the release WRITE a rejection rule for that field at --record. That is not only reading it: measured across spec/.tp-review/, 67 non-PASS rows carry out-of-enum severities (high 16, medium 15, low 36, in cycles 0.29.0, 0.30.0, 0.31.0, 0.31.2 and 0.32.0), so the release makes files that record cleanly today fail to record -- a behaviour change for the field, on a corpus that already contains the case. A reader reconciling §2 with §6 cannot tell whether the validator is in scope, and §6 is where a decomposer looks to decide what NOT to build.
suggestion: Reword Non-Goal 3 to what is actually not changing: 'The vocabulary is unchanged -- no value is added, removed or re-ranked. What this release adds is enforcement of the existing vocabulary at --record.' And say explicitly that the enforcement is audit-side only, since engine.SeverityRank (internal/engine/cluster.go:31-41) implements the REVIEW vocabulary critical|high|medium|low and a validator wired to it would reject every legal audit severity.

finding: Non-Goal 4 (`Touching review convergence. review_converge_on keeps its current behaviour and default`) and §4's reset collide on a shared function, and neither section names it. engine.ConsecutiveClean is not audit-only: internal/cli/review_status.go:91 emits the REVIEW --status payload's `consecutive_clean` from it, and internal/cli/record_idempotent_test.go:138 pins that key. Making ConsecutiveClean hash-aware to satisfy §4 changes the review --status payload and breaks Non-Goal 4; leaving it alone means the codebase carries two different definitions of a trailing clean streak, one hash-aware and one not, on two surfaces that already disagree (review --status uses ConsecutiveClean while review.go:979 and review_record.go:204 use the severity-aware ReviewConsecutiveClean). An implementer cannot choose without deciding whether Non-Goal 4 forbids touching the shared symbol or only the review_converge_on semantics.
suggestion: Restate Non-Goal 4 in terms of observable review behaviour rather than `not touching`, and have §4 name the function it changes or add. If a new audit-side walker is introduced, say explicitly that engine.ConsecutiveClean keeps its current semantics for review.

finding: The repair added a new normative mechanism to §2 and left the section that fences the release's scope contradicting it. §2 now says 'this release's first job' is that 'a non-PASS row whose severity is missing or outside error|warning|info is rejected by --record the way an unknown category is', and that the rule for an unrecognised value 'must be stated normatively and must fail closed'. §6 Non-Goal 3, unchanged, reads: 'Changing severity's meaning or vocabulary. error | warning | info is unchanged; this release ONLY READS IT.' Rejecting a record on the value is not reading it. §1's Overview, also unchanged, still scopes the release to 'the two things review already has: a severity-aware convergence policy, and a reason to distrust a streak that spans a changed spec' -- which named neither §3's disposition rule (a pre-existing gap) nor now the sink validation the body calls the first job. A decomposer reading §1 and §6 for scope will not build the mechanism §2 makes a precondition.
suggestion: Reword Non-Goal 3 to fence only the vocabulary ('the enum error|warning|info is not extended or redefined; this release validates it and reads it'), and update §1 to enumerate what actually ships: sink validation of severity, audit_converge_on, disposition-based exclusion, and the spec-change streak reset.

finding: Round 1's untested-normative-section class was answered by deleting the three sections that carried it; the repair then reintroduced it inside §2, and §7 was not touched. The eight tests are byte-identical to the round-1 snapshot and cover only audit_converge_on resolution/predicates (1-4), the disposition exclusion (5) and the spec-hash reset (6-8). Nothing tests the new sink validation, which §2 states as a precondition for the release's safety ('before the gate reads the field'), with three sub-obligations, none of which is acceptance-testable as written: (a) what --record does to a non-PASS row with a missing or out-of-enum severity, and at which exit code (the sibling `category` path exits through invalidCategoryRows -- the spec does not say the severity path matches it); (b) 'the conservative rule for an unrecognised value must be stated normatively and must fail closed' -- §2 says the rule must be stated and then does not state it; (c) 'the 67 historical rows are what the migration path has to answer for' -- no migration path is specified, and those rows are live corpus that test 4's replay reads.
suggestion: State the rejection rule normatively in §2 (exit code, hint, and the fail-closed default for an unrecognised value) and add §7 tests for it: a non-PASS row with a missing severity is refused; one with an out-of-enum severity (`high`, matching the 67 recorded rows) is refused with the hint naming the legal set; and a test pinning what happens when the validation meets a pre-existing round file carrying those values.

finding: The requirement this round added is the only normative clause in the release with no test, and it is the one the release calls its 'first job'. §2 now states 'This release therefore ships validation at the sink before the gate reads the field'. §7 is byte-identical to round 1: tests 1-4 cover the predicate, 5 the disposition, 6-8 the reset. Nothing asserts that a non-PASS row with an out-of-enum severity is refused, nothing pins the observable of that refusal (its category twin is exit 1 / ExitValidation with recordRowHint and a message naming every offending line at once -- internal/cli/audit_record.go:62-69 and 289-295 -- and §2 promises 'the way an unknown category is' without pinning either), and nothing asserts a PASS row with severity null still records. The word 'before' is also untestable as written: ordering between a validator and a gate has no runtime observable, only a decomposition dependency.
suggestion: Add three tests: (a) --record on a file holding one non-PASS row with severity 'high' exits 1 with a hint naming both the offending line and the legal values, and records no round; (b) all offending lines are named in one message, matching the category sink's one-round-trip contract; (c) a round of all-PASS rows with severity null records unchanged. Express 'before' as a decomposition constraint (the gate task depends on the validator task) rather than as a sentence in §2, or state the observable that would fail if the order were reversed.

finding: Once `blocking` reads severity, the audit merge's tiebreak becomes gate-deciding, and it was written when severity was inert. dedupAuditRows (internal/cli/audit_merge.go:191-203) keys on `role\x00item_id` and keeps the FIRST row it sees, discarding every later duplicate without comparing status, severity or anything else; the sort that follows is only a stable ordering of the survivors. So when one role emits the same item_id twice at different severities -- or the same role's results file is supplied twice after a retried unit, which loadAuditMergeRows accepts -- which severity reaches --record, and therefore whether the round is clean under `blocking`, is decided by input order. The review side does not work this way: its merge picks each cluster's representative by highest severity, then role, then text (skills/tp/REFERENCE.md, `Finding class and Report`). §2 says nothing about the merge path, so an implementer would leave first-wins in place and ship an order-dependent gate.
suggestion: State the audit merge tiebreak for the severity-aware world -- highest severity wins within a (role,item_id) key, matching review -- and add a test. If first-wins is deliberate, say so and say why the asymmetry with review is acceptable now that the value gates a release.

finding: The paragraph the repair inserted at the head of §2 ends 'it is the reason THE SINK VALIDATION ABOVE is a precondition rather than a nicety.' The sink validation is described below it, not above: the inserted paragraph is the first content in §2 (line 30), and the sink-validation paragraph runs at lines 66-72. Nothing above line 30 -- not §1 -- mentions it. The wording is the tell that the paragraph was drafted for the end of §2 and pasted at the head, which is also why it forward-references a mechanism the reader has not met yet and why §2.1's conclusion (see the separate finding) was not carried along with it.
suggestion: Either move the paragraph to the end of §2, after the sink-validation paragraph, or change 'above' to 'below' and add a one-clause gloss so the forward reference is readable on first pass.

finding: §2 is now at least four tasks carrying a hard ordering constraint that exists only as an italicised word, and two of the four have no decidable acceptance today. The constraint: `This release therefore ships validation at the sink BEFORE the gate reads the field`. The four: (1) the audit_converge_on field itself -- resolution, precedence, setter validation, hint (§7 test 1); (2) the severity-aware clean predicate (§7 tests 2-3); (3) sink validation at --record with its exit code and hint; (4) the migration for already-recorded rounds. tp's decomposition expresses ordering as depends_on, so `before` has to become an edge -- but as written it is unclear whether it means commit order within the release (satisfiable) or that the gate must REFUSE to read severity on rounds recorded before validation existed (a runtime condition nobody has specified). Tasks 3 and 4 cannot be given acceptance criteria until the contradiction and the migration reported separately are settled, so a decomposer today can write two of the four.
suggestion: Make the ordering an explicit dependency statement -- the predicate task depends_on the validation task -- and say plainly that it is a build-order constraint with no runtime component, or, if it does have one, specify it. Then settle the two open decisions so tasks 3 and 4 are writable.

finding: '§5 records the same gap from the --check side' no longer holds after §5 was rewritten. §5 now records that the --check divergence section was removed from this release and lives at spec/0.46.0.md §8; it states no gap of its own. A reader following the pointer for the substantive argument -- the one that says --check reports 'not converged' indefinitely while divergence gates nothing -- lands on a removal notice.
suggestion: Point the sentence at spec/0.46.0.md §8 directly, or drop it; §2.0a's own paragraph already makes the point.

finding: §2.0a closes with `§5 records the same gap from the --check side.` That was true of the §5 the round-1 repair deleted (`The gate tp reports and the gate this project ships on are not the same gate`). The §5 that now stands is `What is deliberately not in this release, and why it was here three hours ago`, which records no --check gap -- it records the removal. The material moved to spec/0.46.0.md §8. The reference is the worst kind for tooling: §5 still exists, so a broken-cross-ref check resolves it and reports nothing, while a reader following it lands on a section about deletions. This is the class the repository already warns about after three renumberings -- `a reference that resolves to a file is not thereby correct, because the file's subject may have moved`.
suggestion: Point it at spec/0.46.0.md §8, or delete the sentence -- §2.0a's argument does not need it. Sweep the rest of the release for references to the deleted §5/§5a/§5b at the same time.

finding: §2.0a still ends '§5 records the same gap from the --check side.' This round moved that content out: §5 is now 'What is deliberately not in this release', and it says the --check divergence went to spec/0.46.0.md §8 (verified present: spec/0.46.0.md line 257, '8. The gate tp reports and the gate this project ships on are not the same gate'). A reader following the pointer finds the removal notice naming the gap, not the account of it. The pointer is load-bearing here: it is the sentence that tells the reader the converge-at-round-3-with-rows-surfaced claim has a --check-side counterpart somewhere.
suggestion: Repoint it: '§5 records where that gap went; spec/0.46.0.md §8 states it from the --check side.' Then sweep §2, §2.0a and §2.1 for any other pointer into the removed §5/§5a/§5b -- this is the third renumbering in this repository to leave stale pointers behind, and CLAUDE.md already asks for the sweep after any move.

finding: Re-examining round 1's own grounds, as this round asked. My contested-default row argued for defaulting to `all` partly because "all reproduces the recorded history exactly". That ground does not hold, and I should not have used it: I took the phrase from §2.1's own sentence rather than from the data. It is true of v0.35.0 only -- v0.36.0 has zero clean audit rounds, so `all` reproduces nothing there, it simply never converges. The verdict survives on the other ground I gave (`all` changes no existing project's behaviour); the reproduces-the-history half was a scoping convenience inherited from the text under review. §2.1 still asserts it in the same words, unchanged by the round-1 repair.
suggestion: Strike "reproduces the recorded history exactly" from §2.1 or bound it explicitly to v0.35.0. A default argued from a property holding in one of the two cycles measured is the same defect the section warns about one paragraph later.

finding: §3 names three disposition values and binds them to no key, while the codebase already has two predicates at different granularities and §3 fits neither. The stored shape is written by audit_resolve.go:193-199: `resolved = {status, evidence, resolved_at}`, so the verdict does live at `resolved.status`, and dispositionStatusOf (:203-207) reads it back and returns the literal `unknown` for anything it cannot parse. But the predicate the oracle actually uses, engine.rowDisposed (internal/engine/unitkind.go:250-253), tests key PRESENCE only and cannot distinguish `fixed` from `wontfix` -- and it is shared: nextunits.go:188 skips any disposed audit row when choosing the next audit-fix unit, and unitkind.go:233's allRowsDisposed drives a unit-kind decision. §3 requires a three-way reading (wontfix/duplicate excluded, fixed not), so either a second predicate appears -- and §3 must say which of rowDisposed's two call sites keeps the old binary meaning -- or rowDisposed gains the distinction, in which case a `fixed` row starts generating audit-fix units again. §3 also gives no rule for `unknown`, nor for a recorded `resolved` object carrying no `status` at all.
suggestion: Name the key (`resolved.status`), name the predicate the counting rule uses, say explicitly that engine.rowDisposed keeps its presence-only meaning for the oracle (or that it does not, and what changes at nextunits.go:188 and unitkind.go:233), and give the fail-closed rule for a `resolved` object with a missing or unrecognised status -- consistent with whatever §2 settles for severity.

finding: §5 spends twenty lines arguing against three sections that no longer exist in this document and are already owned by spec/0.46.0.md §8, §8a and §8b. Its operative content is the last sentence, "This release is §2, §3 and §4." Everything before it is a critique of drafts a decomposing agent never sees, and it is paid by every role in every remaining round of this spec -- in the release whose own §5 cites spec length as this repository's strongest measured predictor of cycle cost. The section making that argument is the section paying it.
suggestion: Keep the pointer and the one fact that outlives the drafts (both predicates are over non-PASS rows, so any rule about PASS rows is inert here) and move the rest to the candidates file, where a deferral's reasoning is read by whoever picks it up rather than by every reviewer of every round.

finding: §2 calls sink validation "this release's first job" and makes it a precondition for the gate, and §7's eight tests never mention it: 1-4 are the knob, 5 the disposition, 6-8 the reset. Nothing pins which values are refused, whether absence is refused, the exit code, the hint, whether every offending line is named at once the way the category sink's own guard requires, or what --merge does. Round 1 named this cost exactly -- "a record-path refusal, its exit code, its hint and its test are new surface, not free" -- and the rewrite adopted the mechanism without adopting the budget.
suggestion: Add one numbered test for the sink: the refused values, the accepted ones (including whatever the missing case resolves to), the exit code, and the all-lines-at-once message, mirroring TestCountAuditFindings_RejectsCategoryOutsideTheEnum.

finding: A quantifier the repair itself wrote is wrong. §2: 'Both review arms falsified it independently in round 1.' Round 1 ran four roles and all four filed a critical on this exact claim: review-r1-architect.ndjson (prompt-text-read-as-validation), review-r1-ax-economist.ndjson (unvalidated-agent-label-gates-release), review-r1-implementer.ndjson (unvalidated-field-assumed-validated), review-r1-tester.ndjson (unvalidated-enum-claim). 'Both ... arms' names two, and tp's review panel has no notion of two arms. The undercount weakens the very sentence it appears in -- 4-of-4 independent falsification is a stronger warrant than 2 -- and it is the class CLAUDE.md records as the one that rots silently: a claim of exhaustiveness over a set the author did not enumerate.
suggestion: 'All four round-1 review roles falsified it independently', or drop the count and cite the round: 'review round 1 falsified it from every role'.

finding: Near-miss, self-caught. I had concluded that §2's 'across recorded audit rows, 67 non-PASS rows carry out-of-enum severities (high 16, medium 15, low 36) in the v0.29.0-v0.32.0 cycles' was an instance of CLAUDE.md's uncounted-quantifier class, and was about to report it as an unbound measured constant in a paragraph whose neighbouring claims round 1 had already falsified. Counting every recorded audit row under spec/.tp-review/*/audit-round-*.ndjson before writing the row: 36 low, 15 medium, 16 high, total exactly 67, every one of them inside the stated range (0.29.0 3, 0.30.0 4, 0.31.0 2, 0.31.2 24, 0.32.0 34). The finding would have been false. Worth recording because the wrong conclusion was cheap to reach here -- three claims in the same paragraph were false last round, which makes the fourth feel false too.
suggestion: No spec change. This figure is the model for the rest of §2: a count reproducible from a named artifact, which is exactly what CLAUDE.md asks a quantifier to be.

finding: The paragraph the round-1 repair inserted at the top of §2 refers to its neighbours by position and both references are wrong from where it now sits. It is the FIRST paragraph of §2 and says `it is the reason the sink validation above is a precondition rather than a nicety` -- the sink-validation paragraph is roughly thirty lines BELOW it (§2, `So the safety argument has to be built rather than cited`). It also opens `The table below asks when the loop stops under each predicate`, but the table immediately below it is the three-row claim/what-is-there table added by the same repair; the table it means is in §2.1, past a subheading. An implementer reading §2 top-down meets a precondition referenced before it is stated.
suggestion: Refer to sections by anchor rather than by position -- `the sink validation stated later in this section` or an explicit §2.1 for the cost table -- since inserted paragraphs invert `above`/`below` every time a section is repaired.

finding: §2's opening paragraph reads 'it is the reason the sink validation above is a precondition rather than a nicety'. The sink validation is below it -- the paragraph beginning 'So the safety argument has to be built rather than cited' -- so the back-reference was written for the paragraph's earlier position and survived the round-1 repair that moved it to the top of §2. The same sentence's other pointer, 'The table below', is correct, which makes the wrong one easy to read past.
suggestion: Change 'above' to 'below', or move this summary paragraph to sit after the validation clause it summarises.

finding: An unchanged §2.0a sentence now sits against a repaired §2 that enumerates the same rounds more carefully, and the two disagree. §2.0a: 'v0.36.0's rounds 12 and 13 produced two error-severity findings.' Counted from spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/audit-round-12.ndjson and -13.ndjson: round 12 carries 2 non-PASS rows, both error; round 13 carries 3, of which 2 are error. Four error rows, not two. Round 1 raised this (architect, uncounted-quantifier) and the repair to §2 -- which now correctly says 'v0.36.0's rounds 7, 12 and 13 each carry error rows' -- passed over it. The count matters here because it is the caveat carrying the one case where a severity gate would have stopped a cycle that still had error-severity defects.
suggestion: Say 'four error-severity rows across rounds 12 and 13' or, if the intent is distinct defects rather than rows, say so and give the defect count.

finding: Near-miss, self-caught. While drafting the nonblocking_open finding I had concluded that an executable guard test pins 'nonblocking_open is never an audit field', and was about to cite it as a shipped assertion the spec silently reverses. Reading internal/cli/harness_note_test.go before writing: line 263 is a comment inside TestCompact_AuditOmitsHarnessKeepsNextAction, whose executable assertions cover harness_note, harness_stale and next_action only; every executable nonblocking_open assertion in the suite is review-side (harness_note_test.go:314/322, reviewconvergeon_clean_test.go:107/114, nextaction_test.go:60). The invariant is documented and commented, not asserted. The finding survives on the documentation (spec/0.31.0.md §8.4, skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:634), but the citation I nearly wrote would have been wrong, and it is the kind of wrong that reads as stronger evidence than it is.
suggestion: Whichever way §2.0a's surface question is settled, add the executable assertion that comment stands in for -- absent on audit, or present under the stated condition.

finding: Self-caught. My first form of the §2.1 finding was "rounds 12 and 13 carry error rows, so `all` cannot converge at round 13" -- true, but weak, and it implies rounds 1-11 were clean, which would have licensed a repair that fixed only the last two cells and left the row still wrong. Reading spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/state.json before writing gave the stronger and simpler fact: all thirteen audit rounds carry clean: false, so the trailing clean run is zero for the entire cycle and neither "converged" nor an `all` convergence point exists anywhere in it. The weak version would have passed review.
suggestion: No spec change. The transferable rule for this round: derive a table cell from the state file that computes it, not from the round files it summarises.

finding: Re-examining the rest of round 1's rows. The eight covering §5, §5a and §5b were acted on by removing the sections, and their reasoning holds unchanged -- none claimed the observations were wrong, only that they named no mechanism and carried no acceptance, which is what the new §5 concedes. The §3 row (self-declared-label-opens-the-gate) also stands, and the rewrite gives it sharper ground rather than answering it: §2 now spends its longest passage establishing that a self-declared label must be validated at the sink before it may open a gate, while §3 admits wontfix and duplicate -- written by the same agent, checkable by nothing even in principle -- with no sink at all. The release validates the label that has an enum and leaves unfenced the one that can have none. Filed as re-examination, not as a second finding.
suggestion: No action beyond the open §3 row. If §3 survives review, state §2's standard's disposition for dispositions explicitly, rather than leaving two sections in one release to imply opposite policies about self-declared labels.

finding: Self-caught before writing: on reading internal/engine/nextunits.go:188 -- `if AuditRowIsPass(row) || rowDisposed(row) { continue }` -- I formed the conclusion that tp already excludes disposed rows from audit convergence and that §3 was therefore largely shipped, which would have been reported as a redundancy finding against §3. It is false. That call site is the RESUME ORACLE choosing the next audit-fix unit, not the convergence count; the convergence count is countAuditFindings (internal/cli/audit_record.go:228-257), which increments on `!engine.AuditRowIsPass(row)` with no disposition check anywhere in the function. The two paths deliberately disagree today, which is itself worth stating in the spec: the oracle already stops pointing at a disposed row while the counter still counts it, so §3 is closing a gap between two existing predicates rather than adding a new concept.
suggestion: Record in §3 that engine.rowDisposed already governs unit selection and that this release aligns the counter with it (or deliberately does not, for `fixed`). Reviewers and implementers both land on nextunits.go first because it is the only place the two ideas already meet.

finding: Near-miss, self-caught before recording. Reading the new §5 I formed the conclusion that the removal was cosmetic -- that two round-1 criticals had been closed by deleting their subject and the material had gone nowhere, which would have been a critical 'answered by deletion' finding: 'the three sections were removed with a forwarding sentence to a spec that does not carry them.' Checked before writing: spec/0.46.0.md really does now carry '## 8. The gate tp reports and the gate this project ships on are not the same gate', '## 8a. A PASS row can carry a defect in its note, and the counter cannot see it' and '## 8b. A round recorded with one role erases the counter the ship rule reads' -- the three headings verbatim, in the file §5 names. The move is real, and the deletion is a legitimate answer to the round-1 findings on §5/§5a/§5b, which is why the finding filed instead is narrower: what the move dropped is one clause the REMAINING sections still depend on (the --check requirement), not the sections themselves.
suggestion: No spec change. Note for the merge: the round-1 findings against §5, §5a and §5b should be marked resolved-by-relocation rather than reappearing against 0.37.0, and 0.46.0 §10 ('Written at decomposition, one per item') now owes acceptance for three items it did not have when it was written.

finding: The heading "and why it was here three hours ago" pins a wall-clock offset into a committed artifact. It was already false when the file was saved and cannot be maintained; the only reader for whom it is true is the author on the day. Every other temporal reference in this spec names a round or a version.
suggestion: Name the round: "and why review round 1 removed it".

finding: §5 justifies the removal partly by length: the three sections 'added ~100 of 288 lines ... pushing it across the length threshold this repository measured as the strongest single predictor of cycle cost'. The removal did not restore the property it invokes. The spec is 229 lines, not the ~188 the arithmetic implies, because the same round grew §2 by roughly forty lines of narration about what round 1 falsified. CLAUDE.md's measurement is that specs under 200 lines cost ~8-9 total rounds and specs over 300 cost ~23; 229 is not in the cheap band, so the third bullet's remedy is asserted rather than achieved. The first two bullets (no mechanism, §5a inert) carry the removal on their own.
suggestion: Either drop the length bullet, or make it true by trimming §2's account of the round-1 repair -- the three-claim table and the corpus counts are the durable content; the narration of which draft said what is not.
